title: Counters: three simple rules
summary: Counters are nouns that act like adverbs. You need only about a dozen, you can often use ひとつ、ふたつ instead, and sound changes only affect certain kana.

blocks.text: To count things Japanese puts a **counter** between the number and the thing: 犬 is counted 一匹, a bird 一羽, a sheet 一枚. There are dozens, but only about a dozen are common, and you can pick them up as you go. When you read or hear a number followed by a little word, you already know that little word is a counter.
Rule 1: most of the time you can avoid them
The **native counting** ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ... (一つ、二つ、三つ) needs no counter and works for nearly everything except people and small animals.

blocks.jp: りんごを三つください。

blocks.text: Rule 2: counters are nouns, used in two ways

Counters are **nouns**, so they take の before another noun, just like any noun. But they are also special nouns that can modify a **verb** like an adverb. 猫が三匹いる is literally "cats exist in a three-small-animal way", which is why the sentence ends in a verb.

blocks.en: Three cats are in the garden. (counter + の + noun)
There are three cats. (the counter describes the verb)

blocks.text: The counter describes the verb like an adverb, so the sentence ends in a verb.
Each counter fits a kind of thing. 本 counts long things (pens, bottles), because old books were scrolls, long rolls of paper. 冊 came later for bound books. 羽 counts birds, and 人 counts people.
人 is irregular and very common: one person is ひとり, two people is ふたり. From three on it follows the pattern (さんにん, よにん, ごにん).
Rule 3: sound changes follow a pattern

The sound of a counter changes in a pattern. The numbers 1 and 10 take a small っ with counters in the か, さ, た and は rows (いっかい, じゅっさい, いっぴき). The か and は rows also do it at 6 and 8 (ろっぴき, はっぴき). After 三 a counter often voices: さんびき, さんがい, but not always.
A counter whose first kana **cannot take a dakuten** (the ten-ten) never changes: 枚 (ま), 輪 (り) stay the same after any number. Compare 匹 with 枚:

items: About a dozen common counters: 枚 (flat), 本 (long), 冊 (books), 匹 (small animals), 羽 (birds), 人 (people).
Native counting (一つ、二つ) avoids counters for most objects.
Counters are nouns that can also work like adverbs: 猫が三匹いる.
If the counter's first kana can't take a ten-ten, its sound never changes. Otherwise 1, 6, 8 and 10 often take a small っ, and 3 often voices.
